title: Overcoming Execution Drag in Volatility Harvesting: Hysteresis and Partial PCA Orthogonalization
learned: A self-published (not peer-reviewed) Nifty50 study shows that a volatility-risk-premium strategy that looked good on paper (17.85% gross, Sharpe 1.84) turned into an 18.5% net loss once the cost of constantly re-hedging delta and slippage were counted. Only re-hedging less often (a 'deadband' that ignores small delta changes) and stripping out the index's main market factor brought it back to a claimed 11.44% net, Sharpe 2.03. The takeaway for a retail trader: hedging and trading costs can wipe out an options edge entirely, so trade less often and count costs first.
relevance_note: The cost lesson applies to anyone hedging QQQ/NQ options, but the strategy is Nifty dispersion/stat-arb, data period and cost assumptions are not stated, and it is an unreviewed preprint.

idea.text: Add the volatility risk premium spread (30d implied vol minus 20d realized vol, in logs) as a feature for the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: Arbitrage Scenario in India's Option Market - A mathematical modelling breakdown
learned: Using Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty minute and tick data from January 2025 to April 2026, this self-published paper argues that big institutional selling 'slams' on Wednesday/Thursday expiry afternoons set off retail stop-loss cascades, with a window of about 180-300 seconds between the slam and the peak of the cascade. It claims its 18-model 'Threshold Causal Calculus' suite was right 68.2% of the time during the March 2026 volatility spikes and cut slippage by 85.8% compared with moving-average crossovers. The claims are big, the method is vaguely described, and the comparison is only against a weak baseline.
relevance_note: Indian index expiries, intraday tick timing and an unreviewed, loosely specified model; the general idea that stop cascades cluster on expiry days is plausible for QQQ 0DTE, but nothing here transfers directly or can be checked with daily data.

idea.text: Measure intraday stop-cascade windows (180-300 s after a large institutional move) on QQQ expiry afternoons.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: One Premium in Four Disguises: Volatility Arbitrage, Implied Correlation and the (Apparent) Decay of the Dispersion Premium, 2006–2026
learned: Testing 2006-2026 data, this paper finds that four popular 'volatility arbitrage' trades (implied-vs-realized, VIX calendar, dispersion, skew-gated short vol) are really the same bet: each has a 0.71-0.95 daily correlation with simply shorting VIX futures, and none earns a significant extra return after correcting for testing many variants (best t-stat 2.16, failing a Holm test at p=0.09). The Cboe SKEW index was neither a source of return nor a reliable warning sign. The only add-on that held up out of sample was sizing short-vol positions in proportion to VIX (Sharpe 0.57 to 0.79), and even that is still just the plain variance premium.
relevance_note: Directly useful as a reality check for anyone selling QQQ/NQ premium: fancy vol-arb variants mostly repackage short vol, though the paper is an unreviewed preprint and full text could not be read (only the abstract).

idea.text: Following the paper's claim that SKEW is not a reliable warning: go short QQQ for the next day only when put skew is in the top 10% of its past year, and see if that beats chance.

title: Deep hedging 0DTE options
learned: Using high-frequency SPX option data with real transaction costs, the authors train a reinforcement-learning agent to delta-hedge 0DTE options and find it beats standard Black-Scholes delta hedging at that horizon. The learned hedge kept working during the COVID-19 crash even though it was trained only on calm periods, and the paper also studies how it behaves around price jumps. The abstract gives no headline numbers for the size of the improvement.

title: Stock Market Uncertainty and the Stock-Bond Return Relation
learned: This older study links daily stock and Treasury bond moves to stock-market uncertainty, measured by index option implied volatility and unusually high trading volume. When implied volatility is high, stocks and bonds tend to move less together in the following period, and on days when implied volatility jumps, bonds tend to do well relative to stocks (a flight to safety). In plain terms: bonds diversify a stock portfolio best exactly when fear is high. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
relevance_note: A cross-asset portfolio finding about stock-bond correlation, not a tool for next-day NQ range or QQQ direction, and we have no bond data to check it.

title: Uncovering the asymmetric information content of high-frequency options
learned: The authors split the high-frequency moves of option prices into up-moves and down-moves (semivariances) and signed jumps, using SPY options and 15 single stocks. The downside moves of out-of-the-money calls and the upside moves of OTM puts help predict future volatility, the variance risk premium and next-month excess returns, beyond plain total option volatility. A volatility-timing strategy built on these measures gained up to 206 basis points a year out of sample for a risk-averse investor.
relevance_note: Index-ETF options and volatility prediction are on topic, but the signals need intraday option price paths we do not store, and the payoff is a monthly volatility-timing gain, not a day-trading edge.

title: Decomposing the Theta Cliff: A SIMDEC Filtering of Asymptotic Time-Decay in Long-Call Options with a Real-Money Intraday Illustration
learned: This paper proposes scaling the normal Black-Scholes theta (time decay) by a factor that depends on the stock's sector and market regime, found with a sensitivity-analysis method called SIMDEC. Its main 'evidence' is three real-money long-call positions tracked through eleven intraday snapshots plus output from the author's own AI pipeline. There are no clear performance numbers, and the sample is far too small to show that the adjusted theta predicts anything.

title: Volatility of Volatility and Leverage Effect from Options
learned: The paper builds model-free estimators of how much volatility itself moves around ('vol of vol') and of the leverage effect (prices falling as volatility rises), using high-frequency prices of short-dated options. It extracts spot volatility from the options and corrects for the noise in option quotes. It is a statistics/methods paper: it shows how to measure these quantities precisely, not a trading result, and the abstract has no market numbers.
relevance_note: Vol-of-vol and leverage matter for QQQ option pricing and skew, but this is an estimation method needing intraday option data; a crude daily version did not help the range forecast.

title: Machine Learning-Based Latency-Aware Smart Order Routing for U.S. Treasury Securities
learned: The authors built a machine-learning order router for US Treasuries that tries to account for quotes going stale while an order travels to a venue, and tested it on a simulated order book calibrated to FRED yield volatility. Although the classifier scored 80.1% accuracy, the router beat a simple best-price router on only 2.2% of test rounds and was actually slightly more expensive (6.561 vs 6.548 basis points, t = -3.86). The honest lesson: a high-accuracy model can still make worse decisions when it is confidently wrong on the cases that matter.
relevance_note: Treasury execution on simulated data has nothing to do with NQ/QQQ options or day-trading forecasts; the only takeaway is the general warning that accuracy is not the same as profit.

title: Demand-Based Option Pricing
learned: Because dealers cannot hedge options perfectly, heavy end-user demand for an option pushes its price up, by an amount tied to how much of its risk cannot be hedged away. Using data on actual dealer and end-user positions, the authors show end users are net long index options, especially out-of-the-money puts, which helps explain why index puts look expensive and why the volatility smirk exists. In short, skew is partly a price of demand, not only a forecast of crashes.
relevance_note: A foundational reason why dealer positioning (the basis of GEX) and put skew matter for index options like QQQ/NDX, though it explains option prices rather than giving a next-day trading signal.

idea.text: Measure end-user net demand by strike in QQQ options and relate it to skew changes.

title: High-Frequency Trading and Price Discovery
learned: High-frequency traders help prices find their correct level: their aggressive (liquidity-taking) orders trade in the direction of lasting price changes and against temporary mispricings, even on the most volatile days. Their passive quotes, on the other hand, tend to get picked off by better-informed traders. Their trading direction predicts price moves only over seconds and is tied to public news, market moves and order book imbalance.
relevance_note: Explains microstructure over seconds, far shorter than the bot's daily horizon, and needs order-level data we do not have.

title: Risk Premia in the Bitcoin Market
learned: Bitcoin is far more volatile than the S&P 500 and its options carry a larger variance risk premium (sellers of volatility are paid more). Most of the S&P 500's equity premium comes from mildly negative return days, while for Bitcoin those moderate down moves explain only about a third of its premium. Bitcoin's premia shift between two regimes: in calm markets investors pay more for variance and upside, and in volatile markets the premium is more balanced and smaller.
relevance_note: The comparison with the S&P 500 premium is mildly informative, but the paper is about Bitcoin options and gives no rule for NQ/QQQ trading.

title: Time Series Momentum
learned: Across 58 liquid futures (equity indexes, currencies, commodities, bonds), an asset's own past 1-12 month return predicts its next month: winners keep rising and losers keep falling, with some reversal over longer horizons. A diversified portfolio of these trend trades earned strong returns with little exposure to normal risk factors and did best in extreme markets. Speculators profit from it at the expense of hedgers.
relevance_note: A well-known monthly trend effect on index futures including Nasdaq-type contracts, but it is a monthly, diversified effect; on a single index at a daily horizon it did not beat simply being long.

title: The Determinants of Stock and Bond Return Comovements

title: Option Return Predictability
learned: For single-stock options, the return to writing delta-hedged calls can be predicted from company traits: it is lower for high-priced, more profitable firms and higher for firms with lots of cash, volatile cash flows, new share issuance, distress risk and analysts who disagree. Long-short option portfolios built this way had annual Sharpe ratios above two and stayed profitable after trading costs. Two option-specific factors explain the profits; ordinary stock risk factors do not.
relevance_note: A cross-sectional single-stock options effect based on company fundamentals; it does not apply to an index like QQQ/NDX and our memory has no firm-level data.

title: Revisiting local expansions for zero days-to-expiry option pricing
learned: Same-day-expiry (0DTE) options are hard to price because over a few hours prices move in jumps and lopsided ways that the normal bell-curve model misses. The authors price them with a fast 'local expansion' formula that adds corrections for skew and fat tails, and find that letting jumps follow a fat-tailed (tempered stable) shape prices SPX 0DTE options clearly better than assuming bell-shaped jumps; the method also held up on DAX and Euro Stoxx 50 0DTE options. The abstract gives no specific error numbers.
relevance_note: Worked from the abstract only (no full text available); it is a pricing-model paper that confirms 0DTE tails are fatter than a normal model implies, useful background for QQQ 0DTE traders but it gives no daily trading signal.

title: A New Star Is Born: Does the VIX1D Render Common Volatility Forecasting Models for the US Equity Market Obsolete?
learned: VIX1D is Cboe's index of how much the S&P 500 is expected to move over just the next day, built from the shortest-dated (largely 0DTE) options. The authors find it usually sits below the 30-day VIX but jumps around more, drifts upward during the trading day, and on average overstates the next day's actual move because it contains a risk premium. After a simple adjustment for that premium, VIX1D alone forecast next-day S&P volatility more accurately than the standard HAR forecasting models (the abstract gives no exact error figures).
relevance_note: Worked from the abstract only (no full text available); directly relevant because a one-day options-implied move is exactly what Volta's next-day range forecast is built around, though my test of the premium adjustment added nothing on top of what the brain already uses.

title: Where Does the Hedging Error Go? A Greek-by-Greek Decomposition for At-the-Money 0DTE Options under Heston
learned: The authors split the hedging error of at-the-money same-day (0DTE) options into seven Greek pieces across 1,015 SPY sessions and find gamma explains about 66% of the error's variance and vega about 38%; a delta-hedged position lost 2.41 basis points per session on average (t = -8.87). Most of the error cannot be hedged away by trading faster: about 86% of SPY's one-minute error (85% for SPX) is a fixed floor, and hedging every 10 seconds on tick data still leaves 93-98% of it. QQQ and NDX showed the same ranking, with gamma the biggest source.

title: Harvesting the Volatility Risk Premium: A Learning-to-Rank Approach
learned: The author uses a machine-learning ranker each morning at 10:00 ET to choose which of eight same-day (0DTE) SPX short puts to sell, from 5-delta to 45-delta, or to skip the day, with position size scaled up when 0DTE implied volatility is rich versus recent realized volatility. title: LiveOption: Evaluating LLM Agents in Structured Option Trading with Nonlinear Payoffs
learned: LiveOption is a test bed where six AI language-model agents traded options live in three tasks: hedging or covered-call overlays on stocks, earnings bets, and intraday 0DTE trading over 102 sessions. None beat simply holding the stock in the overlay task, every model had a negative median return on earnings bets, and in 0DTE each model lost on 62-76 of the 102 sessions with medians of -3.20% to -0.26% per session. The few positive 0DTE averages came from a handful of big winning days and turned negative once the real bid-ask half-spread was charged, mainly because agents kept paying time decay (theta) on bought options.
relevance_note: Read the repo's full text; a useful cautionary result that buying 0DTE options without an edge bleeds theta and spread costs, but it evaluates AI agents rather than giving a market signal for NQ/QQQ.

title: Cross‐Market Convergence Trading in Options Order Flow
learned: The authors separate options order flow driven by arbitrage-style 'convergence' trading (using matched calls and puts to build synthetic stock or futures positions when options are mispriced against the futures or spot market) from flow driven by traders with private information. This convergence flow grows as the options-futures mispricing widens and predicts returns in the related market in the opposite direction, unlike informed flow. Foreign investors mostly respond to options-versus-futures mispricing and domestic investors to options-versus-spot mispricing, and traders react more to spot underpricing than overpricing, consistent with limits on short selling.
relevance_note: Worked from the abstract only (no full text available); it appears to study a non-US market with investor-type order flow data, and Volta has no options order-imbalance data, so it is of little direct use for NQ/QQQ.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
learned: This well-known study (Gu, Kelly and Xiu) compares machine-learning methods for forecasting stock returns and finds that trees and neural networks beat standard regressions, in some cases doubling the performance of the best regression-based strategies. Their edge comes from capturing nonlinear interactions between predictors, and every method agreed that the strongest signals are variations on momentum, liquidity and volatility. The abstract gives no other specific figures.

The abstract gives no specific numbers.

title: Does Net Buying Pressure Affect the Shape of Implied Volatility Functions?
learned: Bollen and Whaley show that implied volatility moves with public order flow: when more customers buy options than sell them, implied vol rises, so the shape of the volatility smile is partly driven by demand, not only by expected risk. For S&P 500 index options the biggest driver is buying pressure in index puts, while for single-stock options it is call demand. Delta-neutral option-writing strategies earned abnormal returns roughly matching how far implied vol sat above realized vol. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no specific numbers are available.

title: Momentum crashes
learned: Daniel and Moskowitz show that momentum strategies (buy recent winners, short recent losers) usually pay well but occasionally suffer long, painful losing streaks called momentum crashes. These crashes are partly predictable: they happen in panic states, after the market has fallen and when volatility is high, and they coincide with sharp market rebounds that lift the beaten-down losers. A dynamic version that scales momentum down when its forecast mean is low and its variance high roughly doubled the alpha and Sharpe ratio of plain momentum. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: The paper is about cross-sectional stock momentum, not index day-trading, but its 'avoid trend-following after a selloff in high vol' rule carries over to QQQ timing; in my test it helped plain 20-day momentum yet still fell short of an edge.

idea.text: Trade next-day QQQ in the direction of the 20-day return, but go flat in panic states (20-day return negative and 20-day realized vol in its top 30% of the past year).

They find that the Swiss franc and Japanese yen strengthen against the US dollar when US stocks fall, US bond prices rise and FX volatility increases. This safe-haven behaviour shows up from a few hours to several days, grows non-linearly with volatility and in crises, and was especially strong for the yen in 2008. title: Carry Trades and Currency Crashes
learned: Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen show that the currency carry trade (borrow in low-rate currencies like the yen, invest in high-rate ones like the Australian dollar) earns small steady gains but carries crash risk: its returns are negatively skewed, and across currencies the link between interest-rate gap and skewness is very tight (R-squared of 81%). The crashes come from sudden unwinds when risk appetite and funding liquidity dry up, for example in weeks when the VIX or the TED spread rises. After carry losses, speculators hold smaller positions and pay more for crash insurance (risk reversals), and future crash risk actually falls. Read from the repo's full text.
relevance_note: An FX paper, but its 'crowded positions unwind when VIX jumps' mechanism and 'insurance is priciest right after losses' point echo index options; my equity translation of the post-loss signal did not work.

idea.text: Equity analogue of 'after losses, insurance is pricey but crash risk is lower': go long QQQ for the next day when the 20-day return is negative and put skew is in its top 30% of the past year.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: 211 days, hit 51.2% (always-long 51.2%), avg -15.8 bps/day, t=-0.98, positive in 4/9 years
idea.detail: Built from same-day-close r20 and skew (skew rank over trailing 252 days); the paper's FX and TED-spread data are not in memory.

title: Betting against beta
learned: Frazzini and Pedersen argue that many investors cannot borrow, so they buy high-beta (extra-jumpy) assets to get more market exposure, which bids those assets up and leaves them with lower risk-adjusted returns. A 'betting against beta' portfolio, long leveraged low-beta assets and short high-beta assets, earned significant positive risk-adjusted returns in US stocks, 20 international stock markets, Treasuries, corporate bonds and futures. It does badly when funding conditions tighten, and tighter funding pushes betas toward one. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no return figures are given.
relevance_note: A cross-sectional portfolio factor that needs many assets; it says little about next-day NQ/QQQ moves or options and cannot be tested on Volta's single-index memory.

idea.text: Build a long low-beta / short high-beta Nasdaq-100 constituent portfolio and check its link to QQQ moves.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: By Force of Habit: A Consumption-Based Explanation of Aggregate Stock Market Behavior
learned: Campbell and Cochrane build a model in which people judge their well-being against a slowly moving 'habit' level of consumption, so they become much more risk-averse in bad times when consumption falls close to that habit. This single feature explains why stock prices rise in booms and fall in busts, why high prices predict low returns over long horizons, and why stock market volatility is higher in downturns, and the model tracks much of the history of US stock prices using only consumption data. The repo's text file is unreadable scanned OCR, so this summary is from the abstract only.
relevance_note: A macro asset-pricing theory about multi-year horizons; its 'volatility is higher after declines' point is already captured by Volta's range inputs, and adding recent returns did not help the next-day range forecast.

idea.text: Countercyclical volatility: add the 20-day QQQ return and its negative part (recent drawdown) to the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.530% (+0.2%), better in 3/9 unseen years
idea.detail: Built from the same-day-close r20 column: r20 and min(r20, 0); no consumption data is available to build the paper's habit measure.

title: An Empirical Investigation of Continuous‐Time Equity Return Models
learned: Andersen, Benzoni and Lund fitted continuous-time models to daily equity-index returns and found that a realistic model needs both stochastic (changing) volatility and sudden jumps, with jump frequency that can vary over time. Volatility shocks are strongly negatively tied to returns, so falling markets come with rising volatility (the leverage effect). These same features line up with what index option prices show, such as steep put skew, meaning the options market prices them. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no parameter values are given.
relevance_note: Explains why index options carry put skew and fat tails, which is useful context for pricing QQQ options, but the extra return and jump inputs I could build added nothing to the next-day range forecast.

idea.text: Leverage effect and jumps: add today's QQQ return, its negative part, and a jump flag (today's range more than twice the 20-day average) to the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.2%), better in 5/9 unseen years
idea.detail: Today's return taken as the previous row's y_r (close-to-close return ending today, known at today's close); jump flag from l_rng minus l_rng20 above log(2).

title: Price Formation and Liquidity in the U.S. Treasury Market: The Response to Public Information
learned: Fleming and Remolona studied how US Treasury prices, volume and bid-ask spreads react to major macro announcements. In a brief first stage the price jumps almost instantly while trading volume actually drops and spreads widen sharply, showing prices can reprice to news without much trading. In a longer second stage volume surges, volatility stays elevated and spreads remain somewhat wide as traders reconcile their different readings of the news. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no timing or size figures are given.
relevance_note: The two-stage reaction (instant jump, then lingering volatility) is relevant to trading NQ around CPI or jobs releases, but the paper is intraday Treasury data, and testing whether an event day lifts the following day's NQ range found nothing.

idea.text: Post-announcement persistence: add a flag and the size of the implied event premium for today's session to the next-day NQ range forecast, to see whether volatility lingers into the day after a scheduled event.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.531% (-0.0%), better in 5/9 unseen years
idea.detail: Built from the previous row's event_prem (the options-implied premium for today's session, known before today's close): its log and a flag for values above 1.2.

title: The lead–lag relation between VIX futures and SPX futures
learned: The authors studied how VIX futures and S&P 500 futures move against each other minute by minute. When markets are calm the two are only loosely connected, but when volatility is high they move strongly in opposite directions and VIX futures tend to move first, with S&P futures following. The lead is so short that, after transaction costs, it could not be turned into a profitable strategy; whichever market is relatively more liquid tends to lead, and market-maker hedging also shapes the relation. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no correlation or lag figures are given.
relevance_note: Useful intraday context that VIX moves can front-run index futures in stressed markets, but the effect is seconds-to-minutes and not tradeable after costs, and a daily version of the idea found nothing in my data.

idea.text: Daily vol-leads-price: on high-volatility days (20d realized vol above its trailing median), go short QQQ the next day if 30d IV rose today and long if it fell; also add today's IV change to the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: 1041 days, hit 48.4% (always-long 55.1%), avg -8.3 bps/day, t=-1.51, positive in 2/9 years
idea.detail: Signal = -sign(today's change in l_iv30) on days where l_rv20 exceeds its expanding median up to the previous day; the range add-on (IV change, its high-vol interaction and its absolute size) was also NO EDGE (0.531% -> 0.533%, better in 1/9 years). The paper's effect is intraday, which daily closes cannot capture.

title: Central Bank Participation in Currency Options Markets
learned: The paper asks whether a central bank can calm an exchange rate by trading currency options instead of buying and selling the currency itself. Its key point is that if the central bank sells options, market makers end up long those options and their delta-hedging pushes against price moves (they sell rallies and buy dips), which dampens volatility; selling a strangle can also make a target zone more credible and may cost less than spot intervention, but it exposes the bank to unlimited losses. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no cost or volatility figures are given.
relevance_note: The mechanism (dealers long options hedge in a stabilizing way) is the same logic behind dealer-gamma readings for QQQ, which the brain already uses, but the paper is about FX policy and adding extreme-gamma effects found nothing new.

idea.text: Stabilizing dealer hedging: test whether the effect of dealer gamma on the next-day NQ range is non-linear, by adding flags for very high (top 20%) and very low (bottom 20%) gamma rank plus its square.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.534% (-0.5%), better in 5/9 unseen years
idea.detail: Built from today's gex_rank (known at the close): its square, a flag for gex_rank > 0.8 and a flag for gex_rank < 0.2; the linear gex_rank is already in the brain's base model.

title: Dilemma not Trilemma: The Global Financial Cycle and Monetary Policy Independence
learned: Rey shows there is one global financial cycle: capital flows, credit growth, bank leverage and risky asset prices around the world rise and fall together, and the cycle moves opposite to the VIX (low VIX = money pours in, high VIX = flows collapse). A single global factor explains about 25% of the variation in returns across 858 risky assets worldwide, and in her quarterly VAR a cut in the Fed funds rate is followed by a lower VIX after about 5 quarters and more credit flows after about 12 quarters; other studies she cites find Fed rate shocks explain roughly 20-30% of VIX variation at horizons beyond 7-10 quarters. Her policy conclusion is that with free capital flows, countries lose monetary independence even with floating exchange rates unless they manage capital flows or use macroprudential limits on leverage.
relevance_note: Good macro background on why the VIX regime and Fed policy drive risk assets over quarters and years, but it says nothing usable about next-day NQ moves, and my daily test only rediscovered the market's normal upward drift.

idea.text: Low-VIX regime = risk-on: hold QQQ long the next day only when 30d IV is below its trailing one-year average, flat otherwise.

idea.verdict_before_fix: PROMISING: 1215 days, hit 56.9% (always-long 56.9%), avg +7.8 bps/day, t=2.86, positive in 8/9 years

title: Does herding affect volatility? Implications for the Spanish stock market
learned: Blasco, Corredor and Ferreruela measured herding (traders piling into the same side at the same time) in intraday Spanish stock trades, using the Patterson-Sharma herding intensity measure. They found herding raises volatility in a straight-line way across historical, realized and implied volatility, though the size of the effect differs by measure, and herding variables helped forecast volatility. The repo's text file is only the repository landing page (essentially the abstract), so no effect sizes are available.
relevance_note: Plausible that crowding lifts volatility, but the study is on the Spanish market and needs trade-by-trade order data to measure herding, which I do not have, so it cannot be applied to NQ/QQQ decisions yet.

title: Asymmetric Dynamics in the Correlations of Global Equity and Bond Returns
learned: Cappiello, Engle and Sheppard modelled how volatility and correlations of national stock and government bond indexes change over time, using 15 years of weekly returns (790 weeks, January 1987 to February 2001) and an asymmetric correlation model. Stock indexes get more volatile after bad news than after good news of the same size, while bond volatility shows little such asymmetry; yet both stocks and bonds become more correlated with each other after joint bad news, with stocks reacting more strongly, so diversification shrinks exactly when markets fall. After the euro's launch in January 1999 correlations jumped (bond returns inside the euro area became nearly perfectly correlated) while volatility levels did not break. The repo text was glyph-encoded and was decoded for reading.
relevance_note: Confirms that equity volatility reacts more to down moves and that correlations rise in sell-offs, which matters for hedging, but it uses weekly international data and a daily asymmetric add-on made my next-day NQ range forecast worse.

title: Does Options Open Interest Pin the Underlying? Five Tests on 2,294 Trading Days

title: Institutional Equity Derivatives & Market Microstructure: Analyzing the Mechanics of Option Gamma Exposure (GEX) and its Empirical Impact on Underlying Asset Volatility
learned: This working paper explains Gamma Exposure (GEX): adding up option gamma across the chain tells you roughly how many dollars of stock dealers must buy or sell for each 1% move. When dealers are net long gamma they sell rallies and buy dips, which damps volatility and can pin price near big strikes; when they are net short gamma (often after heavy put buying) they chase the move and can amplify crashes or squeezes. The abstract describes formulas and mechanisms but reports no tested data, sample or numbers. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: The mechanism is central to NQ/QQQ options, but this is an explainer with no empirical results, and Volta already uses dealer gamma rank, so it adds little new; abstract only.

idea.text: Negative-gamma feedback: in the low-gamma regime (gamma rank below 0.2), let today's range surprise and recent losses count extra in the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.533% (-0.4%), better in 5/9 unseen years

title: The Death of Fundamental Analysis? How Option Market Makers Now Dictate Spot Equity Prices

It argues that dealers' mechanical delta hedging anchors prices when they are long gamma and accelerates moves when they are short gamma, and it describes trader tools such as the 'gamma flip' level, call walls and put walls as support, resistance and speed-change zones. No sample, test or numbers are given in the description. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: Duplicate of the GEX explainer already read, with strong claims but no evidence; the gamma-flip and wall levels need strike-level data I do not have.

idea.text: Short-gamma momentum: when dealer gamma rank is below 0.2 (closest proxy for being below the gamma flip), go with the 20-day QQQ trend for the next day; flat otherwise.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: 418 days, hit 46.2% (always-long 58.6%), avg -4.3 bps/day, t=-0.50, positive in 4/9 years

title: Temporal Obfuscation Testing for LLM Structural Reasoning: From Single-Day Dealer Constraints to Persistent Market Regimes
learned: The paper is mainly about checking whether a large language model really reasons or just remembers: it strips dates and tickers from dealer gamma exposure (GEX) data and asks the model to spot hedging patterns from the numbers alone, over 2,221 evaluations from 2020-2025. It reports 91.2% predictive accuracy on single-day patterns, and that raw strike-level data beat pre-computed GEX numbers by 30.8 points (92.3% vs 61.5%). For multi-day regimes, detection rose from 3.7% in 2021 to 100% in 2024 alongside 0DTE growth and GEX size growing from $3.0B to $20.3B, while the related strategy's Sharpe fell from 1.8 to 0.1, which the author reads as a real structure that is no longer profitable. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: Mostly a method for testing AI models; the market takeaways (strike-level beats summary GEX, the gamma edge's Sharpe collapsing to 0.1) are interesting but rest on an LLM-detection setup, not a trading test I can reproduce; abstract only.

idea.text: The paper's signal needs strike-level gamma data and an LLM classifier; my memory only has a single summary gamma rank, which the paper itself says loses much of the signal.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: The Earnings Call Risk and Confidence Analyzer (ERCA)
learned: The authors argue that retail traders buy short-dated options before company earnings calls and lose money when implied volatility collapses after the release, even when they guess the direction right (the 'volatility trap'). They build a complex system (social-media activity model, sentiment indicator, machine-learning forecasters, quarter-Kelly sizing with a 15% drawdown stop) and report on 500 S&P 500 earnings events (2020-2026) that their sentiment-divergence score correlates with the size of the earnings surprise (Spearman 0.48). Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: About single-stock earnings and social-media sentiment, not NQ/QQQ index days; the only transferable lesson is the familiar one that buying options right before a scheduled event pays for IV that usually collapses afterwards.

idea.text: Needs per-company earnings dates, social-media and EPS-surprise data, none of which are in my memory.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: From Arbitrage Removal to Density Extraction: A Model-Free Framework for Short-Dated Options
learned: Very short-dated options (a few hours to a week to expiry) have tiny premiums and wide bid-ask spreads, so mid prices are unreliable and quotes can even seem to allow free-money (static arbitrage) trades. The authors first strip out quotes that would allow such arbitrage at the actual bid and ask prices (ARIES), then fit the smoothest, least-assuming price distribution that stays inside every bid-ask range (SEDEx). On a synthetic Heston test the recovered distribution matched the true one to within about 0.0001 in price, and they apply it to SPXW options from 2012-2023 (five-minute quotes, snapshot 15 minutes before the close) to build short-dated volatility smiles.
relevance_note: A careful tool for reading what 0DTE prices imply about tomorrow's distribution, which could sharpen Volta's implied-move input, but it is a pricing method rather than a trading signal and needs full strike-level option chains I do not store; the repo text ends partway through the empirical section.

idea.text: Building a risk-neutral density needs full bid-ask option chains per strike; my memory only has summary readings (straddle move, IV, skew), so the method cannot be applied.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Differential Machine Learning for 0DTE Options with Stochastic Volatility and Jumps
learned: The author trains a neural network to price 0DTE options and their Greeks under a model with both changing volatility and sudden jumps (Bates), learning prices and Greeks together so that one fast evaluation gives price, delta and gamma. A three-stage training that separately supervises the jump part cut the jump-term error from about 0.093 to 0.014 while keeping price errors similar, and adding jump-sensitivity labels brought the estimated jump intensity much closer to the truth (0.569 vs a true 0.60, compared with 0.739 without them). Everything is on simulated data; the author says applying it to real market data is future work, and notes gamma near the money remains the hardest thing to get right for 0DTE.
relevance_note: A fast-pricing engineering method tested only on simulated data, useful for a market maker hedging 0DTE books but not for Volta's next-day NQ/QQQ decisions.

idea.text: The paper offers a pricing/hedging technique, not a market signal, and it needs option-chain data and simulated paths rather than daily readings.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Real-Time Probabilistic Pricing of Short-Horizon on-Chain Range-Prediction Markets
learned: The paper designs a pricing engine (TESSERA) for crypto 'range-prediction' bets where a user wagers the price stays inside a band for a few seconds to minutes, quoting a payout about once per second from a live price feed. Its volatility estimate is a recency-weighted average with a shock mode, and its anti-exploit rules (re-price on acceptance, kill stale quotes) drive stale-quote leakage from 0.78% to zero in simulation. On simulated data it was well calibrated (0.88% error at a 4.67% house margin), but on real 1-second BTC/USD ticks it failed at first (26% error) until one volatility-floor setting was re-fitted (5.5%), and jumps remained its main weakness.
relevance_note: About seconds-long crypto betting products, not NQ/QQQ options; the only transferable point is that recency-weighted volatility needs per-asset calibration and struggles with jumps.

idea.text: Recency-weighted volatility with a shock mode: add a 10-day half-life EWMA of the daily NQ range and a flag for days whose range is more than double that average to the next-day range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 4/9 unseen years
idea.detail: ewma10 = log of EWMA(half-life 10 days) of exp(l_rng) up to today; shock = 1 if l_rng exceeds log(ewma) by log 2; both use data through today's close.

title: Model Specification and Risk Premia: Evidence from Futures Options
learned: Using S&P 500 futures option prices from 1987 to 2003, the authors find strong evidence that both prices and volatility itself can jump, not just drift smoothly. They also find that investors pay a sizeable, statistically significant premium for protection against those jumps, and say this jump premium is key to understanding why options (especially puts) earn the returns they do. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so the size of the premia is not given.
relevance_note: Explains why index puts are usually overpriced relative to realized moves, useful background for NQ/QQQ option selling or buying, but it is about long-run option pricing (data ends 2003), not a next-day signal; abstract only.

idea.text: Jump-fear premium as a buy signal: hold QQQ long the next day only when put skew (25d put-call IV / ATM IV) is above its trailing one-year median, flat otherwise.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1084 signal days, hit 57.7% (always-long 57.7%), strategy +2.8 bps/day vs +3.6 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds -0.8 bps/day, t=-0.50, positive in 5/9 years
idea.detail: long/flat on `where(rank(skew, 252) > 0.5, 1, 0)` (positive = signal on)

spec.explain: long QQQ when put skew is above its 1-year median, else flat

title: Specification Analysis of Option Pricing Models Based on Time‐Changed Lévy Processes
learned: The authors (Huang and Wu) compare many option-pricing models for S&P 500 index options that are built by speeding up or slowing down a jump process's clock. The best fit needs frequent small jumps in returns and two separate sources of changing volatility, one tied to the jumps and one to the smooth part of price moves. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo), so no fit statistics are given.
relevance_note: A technical model-comparison study for pricing index options; it gives no trading signal or rule for NQ/QQQ day-trading decisions.

idea.text: Comparing option-pricing model structures needs full option cross-sections, not my daily summary readings; there is no simple feature to test.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Crashes, Volatility, and the Equity Premium: Lessons from S&P 500 Options
learned: Santa-Clara and Yan pull two risk measures out of S&P 500 option prices every day: smooth (diffusive) volatility and the expected rate of crashes (jump intensity). Turned into a required return, the premium investors demand for these forward-looking risks averages 70% more than the premium for volatility that actually happened, and this option-implied equity premium significantly predicts later stock market returns. Worked from the abstract only (no full text in the repo).
relevance_note: Directly suggests that options pricing more risk than has been realized signals better future index returns, which I could test on QQQ; the paper's own horizon is longer than one day and it is based on the abstract only.

idea.text: Options-implied premium: hold QQQ long the next day only when 30d ATM IV is high relative to 20d realized vol (log IV minus log RV above its trailing one-year median), flat otherwise.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 1149 signal days, hit 58.5% (always-long 58.5%), strategy +6.3 bps/day vs +3.8 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +2.5 bps/day, t=1.61, positive in 8/9 years
idea.detail: long/flat on `where(z(log(atm30) - log(rv20), 252) > 0, 1, 0)` (positive = signal on)
idea.verdict_before_fix: PROMISING: 1137 days, hit 58.4% (always-long 58.4%), avg +12.7 bps/day, t=3.40, positive in 8/9 years

spec.explain: long QQQ when 30d ATM IV - 20d RV is above its 1-year median, else flat

title: Short‐Selling Bans Around the World: Evidence from the 2007–09 Crisis
learned: Beber and Pagano study the short-selling bans that regulators around the world imposed in 2007-09, using the fact that bans started, ended and applied differently across countries and stocks. Banned stocks became much less liquid: in the U.S. their median bid-ask spread rose 243% versus 54% for exempt stocks, and a covered-short ban added roughly 1.6-2.0 percentage points to spreads against a 3.9% average, with the damage about three times larger for stocks without listed options. Bans also slowed price discovery, especially in falling markets, and did not hold prices up, except possibly for U.S. financial stocks. The repo text covers the liquidity results and the start of the price-discovery section.
relevance_note: A regulatory/liquidity study of a past crisis; no current NQ/QQQ signal, beyond the general point that listed options cushion liquidity when shorting stock is restricted.

idea.text: Needs data on short-selling regimes and stock-level spreads, which are not in my daily index memory.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Ultra-short-term volatility surfaces
learned: Options expiring within a week now make up about 70% of SPX option volume (2023), and their at-the-money implied volatility jumps around from one expiry to the next instead of forming a smooth curve, which classic pricing models cannot fit. Bandi, Fusari, Gazzani and Renò propose Edgeworth++, a jump model with flexible volatility plus a per-expiry shift, that prices all six shortest SPX expiries together quickly in closed form. On 247 trading days (May 2022-May 2023, sampled at 10:30, FOMC days removed) its average error was about 1.0 volatility point, against 1.9 for a two-factor Heston-jump model and 2.8 for a rough-Heston model, with roughly 37-38% of its prices inside the bid-ask spread.
relevance_note: Shows that day-to-day differences between 0-7 day implied vols are real structure rather than noise, which matters for reading QQQ/NQ short-dated IV, but it is a pricing model needing full option surfaces, not a next-day trading signal.

idea.text: The model needs the full set of 0-7 day option smiles each day; my memory has only a 7d/30d IV ratio (already in the brain), not the per-expiry term structure the paper studies.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Inferring Latent Market Forces: Evaluating LLM Detection of Gamma Exposure Patterns via Obfuscation Testing
learned: Regan and Xie fed an AI language model end-of-day SPY dealer-gamma numbers for 242 trading days of 2024, with dates and tickers hidden, and asked whether it saw dealer-hedging patterns; it flagged one 71.5% of the time (100% when given hints), and they say 91.2% of flags 'materialized'. But by their own concrete test (next-day move above 0.3% or intraday range above 1%) only 41.6% materialized, every single day in the sample was classed as negative gamma, and gamma only weakly predicted volatility two days later (p=0.042 at lag 2, not significant at lags 1, 3, 4, 5). Net profit after costs faded from +16 bps in Q1 to 0 by Q4.
relevance_note: Mostly about testing an AI's reasoning, with loose success criteria, one year of SPY and no gamma variation in the sample, so it adds little for NQ/QQQ trading; the one concrete claim (gamma predicts volatility 2 days later) did not hold in my memory. (A duplicate queue entry of the same paper, openalex:W7117127131, was removed too.)

idea.text: Paper claims dealer gamma predicts realized volatility with a 2-day lag: add yesterday's and the day before's dealer gamma rank as features to the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.532% (-0.1%), better in 2/9 unseen years
idea.detail: gex_rank shifted by 1 and 2 market days (known at today's close); a 'gamma rank below 0.2' threshold flag (the paper's 'presence not size' claim) was also NO EDGE: 0.531% -> 0.534%, better in 5/9 years.

title: Profitability of selected 0DTE index options strategies
learned: This study back-tested two versions of a same-day (0DTE) Iron Condor on SPX options, using one-minute index and option prices over 12 months, and reports that both versions were profitable. The authors link this to 0DTE implied volatility being priced higher than the volatility that actually followed, so option sellers collected a premium. Only the abstract was available, so the size of the profits, costs and drawdowns is not known.
relevance_note: The topic (selling 0DTE index premium) is directly relevant to QQQ/NQ options, but I worked from the abstract only (no full text): one year of SPX data with no numbers given is too thin to trust, and it says nothing about tail losses.

idea.text: Selling a same-day iron condor pays when the realized move stays inside the options-priced move; my memory has only daily close-to-close returns and daily ranges, not intraday option prices or the condor's strikes, so the strategy itself cannot be simulated with idea_lab.
idea.verdict: PROMISING (stress test: survived) : power 'inside_day' (base 11%): lowest-fifth days 2% vs highest-fifth 19%, Brier skill +3.4%, better than the base rate in 8/9 unseen years
idea.detail: `rank(impl / rng, 252)` as a predictor of 'inside_day' (inside day) | stress: skill +3.40; nudged formulas kept >= half the skill in 2/2; stale copies (lag 1-12 months) clearly worse in 4/4

spec.explain: higher implied move relative to today’s range predicts the day staying inside the iron‑condor width

title: Local Estimation for Option Pricing: Improving Forecasts with Market State Information
learned: Federal Reserve researchers keep standard option-pricing models (Heston-Nandi GARCH and Heston stochastic volatility) but fit them giving more weight to past days that look like today, measured by VIX, recent realized volatility or simply how recent the day is. On S&P 500 options (14-183 days to expiry, 2011-2023, tested out of sample 2015-2023), this beat the usual equal-weight fit: for the GARCH model the VIX-weighted fit had the lowest implied-volatility forecast error with a Diebold-Mariano t-stat of -5.85 against the benchmark. Gains were largest in calm periods like 2017 and small after 2019 or in high-volatility stretches.
relevance_note: A sound modelling idea (let the model's settings depend on the current volatility regime), but it is about pricing 2-week-to-6-month SPX options, not next-day NQ moves, and the gains mostly faded after 2019.

idea.text: Let the brain's range forecast depend on the volatility regime: add the options-priced move and the 5-day range each multiplied by how high 30d IV is versus its own past, a crude stand-in for the paper's VIX-weighted fitting.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.557% -> 0.557% (+0.1%), better in 5/8 unseen years
idea.detail: z = l_iv30 minus its expanding mean (min 250 days, past data only); features l_bot*z and l_rng5*z. idea_lab cannot reweight training days, so this interaction is only an approximation of the paper's method.

title: Risks and Hedges of Providing Liquidity in Complex Securities: The Impact of Insider Trading on Options Market Makers
learned: This 2009 law-journal article by Stanislav Dolgopolov argues that options market makers lose more from insider trading than stock market makers, because they must quote both sides, carry leveraged non-linear positions and hedge their greeks (delta, gamma, vega), so a trader with secret news can pick them off before a big price jump. It reviews US court cases on whether options traders can claim damages and sketches how such losses could be calculated. It is a legal analysis with no market data or numbers.
relevance_note: Not relevant to NQ/QQQ day-trading decisions: it is about legal liability for single-stock insider trading; the saved text was only the journal's landing page, so I worked from the abstract.

idea.text: No trading signal; the paper is legal analysis about damages from insider trading in single-stock options.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Volatility Parametrizations with Random Coefficients: Analytic Flexibility for Implied Volatility Surfaces
learned: Standard curve formulas used to describe the implied-volatility smile (SABR, SVI) often cannot match very short-dated options, so the authors let one formula parameter be random, which turns the smile into a blend of two curves while staying arbitrage-free and fast to compute. On SPX options on 31 July 2024, the fitting error for the August 2024 expiry fell from 4.8e-4 (regular SABR) to 1.2e-5 (randomized SABR), and the needed randomness shrank as expiry got longer. A variant that randomizes the spot price fits the W-shaped smiles seen in near-expiry AMZN options on an earnings day (April 2018), when the market prices two possible outcomes.
relevance_note: A curve-fitting tool for option quants; it can help read event-day smiles (two-humped price outcomes before earnings), but it gives no next-day signal for NQ/QQQ and the evidence is a few snapshot days.

idea.text: The method needs full option chains per strike and expiry to fit smiles; my memory has only summary readings (ATM IV, 25-delta skew, term ratio), so smile shape (e.g. W-shapes before events) cannot be measured.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Derivatives and Market (Il)liquidity
learned: Huang, Yueshen and Zhang (JFQA 2023) build a theory model of how options and other non-linear derivatives change liquidity in the underlying stock or index. Informed investors who expect calm markets sell derivatives, and when buyers and sellers delta-hedge, the hedging trades dilute informed trading, so each trade moves the price less (liquidity looks better). Whether prices bounce back after moves depends on the derivatives' gamma, and the model warns that usual illiquidity measures may not line up with the liquidity risk premium once derivatives trade. It is pure theory with no numbers, and only the abstract was available.
relevance_note: A theory paper (worked from the abstract only, the saved text was the journal page) that supports the general idea that dealer gamma shapes whether moves reverse, but it gives no concrete, testable numbers for NQ/QQQ.

idea.text: The paper's prediction (hedging gamma changes how much price moves reverse) would need intraday price-impact and reversal data; my memory has only daily readings and outcomes, and the dealer-gamma link to next-day range is already in the brain via gex_rank.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: The Joint Cross Section of Stocks and Options
learned: An, Ang, Bali and Cakici looked at US stocks from 1996 to 2011 and found that stocks whose call implied volatility rose most over the past month went on to beat those where it fell most by about 1.09% per month (t=3.45), while stocks whose put implied volatility rose most lagged by about 0.42% per month (t=-2.03). The effect lasted up to six months and fits the idea that informed traders act in options first. In the other direction, stocks that had risen tended to see their option implied volatility climb the next month even as realized volatility fell.
concepts: call and put implied volatility changes
relevance_note: It is a stock-picking result (ranking thousands of single stocks against each other each month), which does not translate directly to timing one index like QQQ the next day; my index-level version of the idea showed nothing.

idea.text: Index version of the paper's put-IV signal: be short QQQ for the next day when 30d implied vol has risen over the past month and long when it has fallen.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: 2001 days, hit 51.6% (always-long 56.6%), avg +4.2 bps/day, t=1.28, positive in 5/9 years
idea.detail: signal = -sign(l_iv30 today minus l_iv30 21 market days ago); also tried -sign(21-day change in 25d skew): NO EDGE (t=0.51, 4/9 years), and both changes as range-forecast features: NO EDGE (0.531% -> 0.532%, better in 3/9 years).

title: The VIX Premium
learned: Ing-Haw Cheng (Review of Financial Studies, 2019) measures the 'VIX premium', the extra price VIX futures carry over the VIX level expected at expiry, and finds it predicts VIX futures returns almost one-for-one (coefficient 0.92) over 2004-2015. Puzzlingly, the premium falls or stays flat when risk rises, and a falling premium warns of higher risk ahead: a one-standard-deviation drop predicted about 3 points more S&P 500 realized volatility. Shorting VIX futures only while the premium was positive raised the Sharpe ratio from 0.57 (always short) to 0.87.
relevance_note: Directly about pricing of volatility risk on the US index; the VIX-futures strategy is not something my data covers, but its core message (a negative or vanishing volatility premium marks risky periods) maps onto QQQ and tested well in my memory as a direction filter.

idea.text: Use the sign of the volatility premium as a risk switch: long QQQ for the next day when 30d implied vol is above 20d realized vol, short when it is below.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 2226 signal days, hit 54.2% (always-long 56.6%), strategy +9.6 bps/day vs +2.1 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +7.5 bps/day, t=2.44, positive in 7/9 years
idea.detail: long/short on `sign(vrp)` (positive = signal on)
idea.verdict_before_fix: PROMISING: 2226 days, hit 54.2% (always-long 56.6%), avg +9.6 bps/day, t=3.16, positive in 9/9 years

spec.explain: long QQQ when volatility premium is positive (implied vol > realized vol), short when it is negative

title: Short‐Term Market Risks Implied by Weekly Options
learned: Andersen, Fusari and Todorov (Journal of Finance, 2017) use weekly S&P 500 options, which mostly price the risk of sudden moves over the next few days, to measure how much the market fears a crash separately from overall volatility. They find this downside-jump fear moves on its own, is not captured by the VIX level, and helps predict future equity returns, so it can flag nervous periods that a calm volatility reading misses. Only the abstract was available, so the size of the effect is not known.
relevance_note: Short-dated index options and crash fear are core to QQQ/NQ options trading, but I worked from the abstract only (no full text), and my rough proxy of 'crash fear not explained by volatility' showed nothing.

idea.text: Proxy the paper's tail-fear factor as the part of 25d put skew not explained by 30d IV, and go long QQQ for the next day when it is above its past-year norm (higher tail fear earns a premium), short when below.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 2226 signal days, hit 51.3% (always-long 56.6%), strategy -1.2 bps/day vs +0.6 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds -1.8 bps/day, t=-0.57, positive in 6/9 years
idea.detail: long/short on `z(rr25 - (atm30 * 0.5), 252)` (positive = signal on)

spec.explain: long when tail-fear factor (skew not explained by IV) is above 1-year norm, short when below

title: The Time–Target Trade-off in Expiry-Day Call Option Buying: Evidence from a Rule-Based Intraday Strategy in the Indian Index Derivatives Market
learned: Two Indian researchers logged 24 expiry-day trades buying index call options around 2:00 PM and selling later that afternoon: 14 made money, 9 lost and 1 was flat, with a median gain of about 3.7% but a range from -95% to +77% of the premium paid. The average trade lasted about 25 minutes, and longer holds tended to do worse (correlation about -0.55 between holding time and return), while higher India VIX did not help (correlation about -0.31). The authors suggest smaller profit targets and short holds, but admit the sample is tiny.
relevance_note: Expiry-day call buying is close to what 0DTE QQQ traders do, but 24 trades from one Indian market with no control group is far too little evidence to act on; mainly a reminder that late-day 0DTE buying can lose almost the whole premium.

idea.text: The study is about minutes-long intraday option trades; my memory has one row per day with no intraday option prices, so the holding-time effect cannot be tested.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Profitability of technical stock trading: Has it moved from daily to intraday data?
learned: Stephan Schulmeister (WIFO, 2008) ran 2,580 moving-average and momentum trading rules on the S&P 500. On daily prices their average yearly gross return fell from 8.6% (1960-71) to about zero in 1983-91 and -5.1% in 1992-2000, so daily chart rules stopped working. The same rules on 30-minute S&P futures prices still made about 7.2% a year gross from 1983 to 2007 (contrarian rules 9.1%, trend rules 4.8%), with roughly 0.01% cost per trade assumed, though results weakened in 2001-07.
relevance_note: Relevant as a caution for index day-traders (simple daily chart rules on US index futures have been dead since the 1990s, edge moved intraday and was fading by 2007), but the data ends in 2007 and my memory cannot test 30-minute rules.

idea.text: Check the paper's daily-data claim on QQQ: follow the 20-day trend (long if the last 20 days were up, short if down) for the next day.
idea.verdict: NOT CONFIRMED on my data: 2227 signal days, hit 53.1% (always-long 56.5%), strategy +4.5 bps/day vs +2.8 for the same average exposure held constantly -> timing adds +1.7 bps/day, t=0.49, positive in 5/10 years
idea.detail: long/short on `r20` (positive = signal on)

spec.explain: go long when the 20‑day return is positive, short when it is negative

title: Two are better than one: Volatility forecasting using multiplicative component GARCH‐MIDAS models
learned: This paper (Conrad and Kleen) studies GARCH-MIDAS models, which split market volatility into a fast-moving short-term part and a slow long-term part driven by an economic series, and works out their statistical properties. On S&P 500 data, the version whose long-term part is driven by US housing starts beat many rival models (HAR, realized GARCH, HEAVY, regime-switching GARCH) when forecasting volatility 2 and 3 months ahead. Only the abstract was available, so the size of the improvement is not known.
relevance_note: Worked from the abstract only; the gains are at 2-3 month horizons, far from next-day NQ ranges, and a slow long-term volatility component added nothing to my next-day forecast.

idea.text: Add a slow long-term volatility component (the average NQ daily range over the last 120 trading days, in logs) to the next-day range forecast, next to the existing 1-, 5- and 20-day ranges.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.530% -> 0.531% (-0.2%), better in 4/9 unseen years
idea.detail: l_rng120 = log of the trailing 120-day mean of exp(l_rng), past data only; adding a 250-day version too was also NO EDGE (0.557% -> 0.557%, 3/8 years). The paper's housing-starts driver is not in my memory.

title: Benchmark dataset for mid‐price forecasting of limit order book data with machine learning methods
learned: This paper (the FI-2010 dataset by Ntakaris and co-authors) publishes a free benchmark dataset of limit order book data for five stocks on Nasdaq Nordic over 10 trading days, about 4 million samples, so machine-learning methods for predicting the next mid-price move can be compared fairly. It also sets a day-by-day cross-validation protocol and gives baseline model results. Only the abstract was available, so the baseline accuracy numbers are not known.
relevance_note: Not relevant to my decisions: it is a dataset for millisecond-level order book prediction on five Nordic stocks (worked from the abstract only), nothing about NQ/QQQ options or daily ranges.

idea.text: Needs tick-level order book data, which my daily memory does not have.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Option Volume Imbalance as a predictor for equity market returns
learned: Michael, Cucuringu and Howison (Oxford) build an 'option volume imbalance': bullish option volume (call buys plus put sells) minus bearish volume (call sells plus put buys), divided by the total, using Nasdaq Options Market and PHLX data from 2015 to 2019 split into five trader classes. Trading the sign of this imbalance predicted next overnight excess returns of mostly single stocks, with the strongest signal coming from market-maker volume, most of the information in high-implied-volatility contracts, and puts more informative than calls. The paper reports results as Sharpe ratios of hypothetical long/short portfolios rather than one headline number.
relevance_note: A plausible source of edge for overnight direction (and it uses Nasdaq exchange data), but it targets the cross-section of single stocks, ends in 2019, and needs signed volume by trader class, which I do not have.

idea.text: Would need daily signed QQQ/NDX option volume split by buyer/seller and trader type; my memory has no option volume or flow columns.
idea.verdict: not testable with my data yet

title: Event‐Day Options
learned: This paper (Jonathan Wright) uses the new options on US Treasury futures that expire every Wednesday and Friday to measure how much interest-rate uncertainty the market prices for a single Fed (FOMC) decision or jobs report. It compares the implied variance the night before those events with the same weekday when nothing is scheduled, compares that priced uncertainty with what actually happened, and builds the implied probability curves on event eves. Only the abstract was available, so the measured sizes are not known.

title: What is the Expected Return on the Market?*
learned: Ian Martin (Quarterly Journal of Economics) shows that index option prices give a lower bound on the stock market's expected return above cash, via a volatility index he calls SVIX. The bound averages about 5% a year but swings wildly, rising above 20% at the height of the 2008 crisis, and predictive regressions do not reject the idea that it is roughly the true equity premium. He argues that the high expected returns available in stressed, high-volatility periods are concentrated over the very short run, and he also derives a market-crash probability and 'simple variance swaps' traded on SVIX.

idea.text: Proxy SVIX with Nasdaq 30-day ATM implied vol and go long QQQ for the next day only when it is above its trailing one-year median (high option-implied premium), staying flat otherwise.

title: The Impact of Market Maker Competition on Market Quality: Evidence from an Options Exchange
learned: This study tracked market makers entering and leaving 134 Australian stock option classes from 2000 to 2006. Adding a dealer improves things most in the liquid classes, so more market makers do not automatically mean better prices in thinly traded options.
relevance_note: This is about exchange market-maker competition in Australian single-stock options in the early 2000s; it says nothing usable about NQ/QQQ moves or day-trading decisions, and QQQ options are among the most competitively quoted in the world.

Tracking these benchmarks also makes the market less liquid and more volatile than if the same investors only cared about where they ended the day.

In plain terms, recent overall volatility already tells you most of what jumps would add.

idea.text: Add a daily jump proxy (how far today's close-to-close QQQ move exceeded two daily standard deviations of 20-day realized vol) to the next-day NQ range forecast.
idea.verdict: NO EDGE: range-forecast miss 0.531% -> 0.531% (+0.0%), better in 5/9 unseen years
idea.detail: Jump = max(|today's return| - 2*daily vol, 0) / daily vol, where today's return is the previous row's y_r and daily vol = exp(l_rv20)/sqrt(252); nonzero on about 5% of days.

title: The Price of a Smile: Hedging and Spanning in Option Markets
learned: Using daily S&P 500 index options from 1986 to 1995, the authors test whether options beyond the at-the-money one carry information that the index and ATM option alone cannot replicate. After the 1987 crash, out-of-the-money and in-the-money options (they look out to 4% from the money) clearly add information at any confidence level, while before the crash they were redundant (only 34% confidence). In plain terms, the shape of the smile prices a separate risk such as volatility shocks or jumps, so models that just bend the volatility curve to fit prices miss something.
relevance_note: Useful background on why put skew is its own risk signal rather than a restatement of ATM IV, but it is a pricing-theory test on 1986-95 S&P options with no direct trading rule for NQ/QQQ.

idea.detail: skew_z = (skew - trailing 252-day mean) / trailing 252-day std (min 126 days), plus skew_z * l_iv30; all known at that day's close.
